text: Room opened — goal: Deliver: Push link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day (the access gate)

name: Reel
text: Publish a *public changelog* for every Kaedim tool update. This forces us to keep links fresh and visible—no hidden changes, no stale docs. The trade-off: we expose internal fixes publicly, but that pressure keeps us honest and speeds up fixes.

name: Scriv
text: Publishing every internal fix risks turning the changelog into noise—users won’t distinguish critical updates from noise, and competitors will exploit our transparency to cherry-pick weaknesses. Instead, ship a *public-facing* changelog that only surfaces user-facing changes, paired with an internal log for engineering; this keeps pressure on freshness without exposing vulnerabilities. Settle it by running a 2-week trial: compare user confusion metrics and competitor exploit attempts before committing.

name: Chisel
text:
We should publish a public changelog that includes every user-facing change, along with a brief description of the update. This forces us to prioritize and communicate clearly about the changes that matter most to our users, which in turn helps push link coverage toward 100%. The trade-off is that we're accepting a potential increase in support queries, as users may ask about changes that don't directly affect them, but this is offset by the increased transparency and trust we build with our user base. By doing this, we're making a conscious decision to prioritize user trust over potential support overhead, which is essential for achieving our goal of pushing link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day.

name: Sift
text: The risk isn’t noise—it’s that a "user-facing" changelog still lets us hide the *why* behind links. If we only surface what users see, we miss the internal fixes that break links but don’t touch the UI. The real test: demand *every* changelog entry—internal or not—include the exact link it fixes. If the bus task can’t verify that, the coverage gate stays shut.

name: Scope
text: **Decision:** Publish a single, unified changelog that lists *every* link change—internal or user-facing—with the exact URL it fixes. This forces us to audit every link weekly, exposing hidden breakages before they rot. The trade-off: users see noise, but that’s the price of forcing link discipline. Without this, we’ll keep hiding fixes until they pile up and break the access gate.

name: Scriv
text: The unified changelog dumps *all* link changes on users—including internal fixes that never affect them—turning the changelog into a dumping ground. That’s not noise; it’s *irrelevance*, and users will ignore it entirely, defeating the purpose. Instead, publish two changelogs: one public for user-facing changes, and one internal for link audits—then auto-merge them into a single internal artifact for compliance. The test: if the public changelog doesn’t drive link discipline, the internal one must.

name: Echo
text: DECISION: Publish two changelogs—one public (user-facing changes only) and one internal (all link fixes, visible to team only)—with each entry including the exact URL it fixes. The public changelog keeps users informed without noise; the internal one enforces weekly link audits. Ownership: Product team delivers the public changelog; Engineering owns the internal one with automated weekly link checks.
